2.text: “There, you Cossacks, come and take it from me.” One of the commanders

3.text: of the Cossacks came, and suddenly wrenched the bottle from Čêpaˊt’s hand.

4.text: Then he spilled the contents on the snow. Now, to spill brandy on the

5.text: ground is considered in those countries perhaps worse than to spill blood.

6.text: Čêpaˊt grew angry and gave the offender a box on the ear, which sent him

7.text: spinning to the ground. A scuffle ensued. Čêpaˊt was arrested, and another

8.text: Chukchee was killed by the Cossacks. I saw Čêpaˊt being dragged by several

9.text: Cossacks to the block-house which was to serve as a temporary prison. He

10.text: had blood on his face, but his spirits were quite undaunted. One of the

11.text: Cossacks (the “private commander” of Sredne-Kolymsk) drew his revolver and

12.text: pointed it at the prisoner’s breast. He said, “I will kill you this instant, you

13.text: dog!” — “Do it!” retorted Čêpaˊt in his usual tone. “I am not afraid, and

14.text: you are a bad one.” All the natives were expelled from the fort, and the

15.text: gate was closed; but a number of Chukchee came to the fence, headed by

16.text: Qančiuˊ, Čêpaˊt’s brother. Very soon the Russians saw that it was necessary

17.text: to free Čêpaˊt. Some of them invited him to make excuses to the commander

18.text: of the Cossacks for the blow, but he flatly refused to do so. “You are all

19.text: bad,” he said quite openly, “Leave me alone.” Then he jostled away the

21.text: These men were of Maritime origin, but the Chukchee who was killed

22.text: in the scuffle was a Reindeer man. He was from the Chaun River, had

23.text: some influence over his neighbors, but even by them he was called “bad.”

24.text: The day before his death he came to the fort and boldly tried to rob a

25.text: Russian creole of some iron knives and spear-heads. This was prevented, but

26.text: he was left unmolested. The next morning he was first to take part in the

27.text: brawl after the arrest of Čêpaˊt. Then the Russians, in their turn, saw their

28.text: chance, took advantage of it, and he was killed.

29.text: Akɪmluˊkê, from the Wolverene River, was also a reindeer-breeder of the

30.text: eˊrmečɪn type. He was good at all kinds of sport, quick-tempered, dexterous,

31.text: and none of his neighbors cared to pick a quarrel with him. The influence

32.text: of a Reindeer Chukchee eˊrmečɪn among the neighboring camps, however, is

33.text: of a rather indefinite kind, because each camp lives its own independent life,

34.text: and has little to do with any of the others.

35.text: In the Maritime villages, where the people live in closer contact, the

36.text: influence of an eˊrmečɪn is more real. When passing with our dogs through

37.text: the Chukchee village Valkaˊʟ̣ên, we wanted to rest our teams, and therefore

38.text: made a stay of two days. One of the inhabitants, Čaˊnla by name, made

39.text: our acquaintance, and offered to sell us a large bag of seal-blubber, with

40.text: which to season the food of our dogs. Being Russians and considered as

41.text: “rich,” we had to buy the larger part of the food for our dogs. The poorer

42.text: men usually get it from their hosts without pay. Moreover, we fed our dogs
